rows.binding_gloss: āśā as grasping / clinging hope — goaded toward a specific outcome or object; the downward pull of attached desire
rows.liberating_gloss: aspiring hope held WITHOUT attachment — forward-orientation that acts while releasing the grip on the result (oriented toward the Great, not the object)
rows.classical_or_philosophical_association_v: ka = Kārya Brahma (the expressed / created universe; Saguṇarasātmaka Brahma; controller of the living world); 'that which produces sound'; 'water' / flowing water (va = water in general); 'hair on the head' (kesha = ka+iisha, also a name of Nārāyaṇa); Buddhist Saṃvṛtti Bodhicitta. These are cosmological / etymological ASSOCIATIONS of ka, NOT poles.
rows.primary_text_citation: Sarkar: Ka = acoustic root of the abhiipśātmaka āśā vṛtti (the propensity of hope), which goads creatures — especially humans — to work in various ways. Ka is ALSO the acoustic root of Kārya Brahma (the expressed universe). Etymology: ka (kae + ḍa) = 'that which produces sound'; also 'water' (flowing water; va = water in general); also 'hair grown on the head' (kac = glossy). Ka + iisha = kesha (hair; also Nārāyaṇa). Kārya Brahma (Saguṇarasātmaka Brahma), represented by ka, is the controller of the living world; Buddhist Saṃvṛtti Bodhicitta = the created world = Kārya Brahma (kāpālika: 'Kaṃ saṃvṛtti bodhicittaṃ pālayati').
rows.attested_vs_authored_verbatim: ATTESTED: ka = āśā vṛtti (hope that goads action) AND ka = Kārya Brahma (expressed universe) + sound/water/hair associations. AUTHORED: the binding/liberating SPLIT of hope (grasping vs non-attached) applies the general attachment principle — the source states āśā goads action but does not itself split it into poles.

rows.binding_gloss: cintā as anxious rumination — the mind churning over unresolved contingencies and personal consequences (e.g. worrying through the late-train inconveniences), gripping the what-ifs
rows.liberating_gloss: cintā as composed, impersonal reflection — holding an unsettled situation open without forcing premature closure; objective contemplation in which one is 'not a direct player' (e.g. weighing how a failing industry might be revived), reflection without anxious grip
rows.classical_or_philosophical_association_v: Paired with ka: ka = āśā (hope) goads action; kha = cintā (worry / objective thought) reflects. kha MEANS 'sky' and 'heaven' but is NOT their acoustic root — the SKY's root is ha; kha = the CRUDE aspects of heaven, while the transcendent sphere = kṣa (ksha). Structurally ka + ha = kha (hence kha follows ka, the first consonant / Kārya Brahma, in the alphabet). These are meanings/associations, NOT poles.
rows.primary_text_citation: Sarkar: The acoustic root of āśā vṛtti is ka; that of cintā vṛtti (the propensity of worry) is kha. If your train runs late you think not only of the delay but of the probable inconveniences (the host, arriving late for food, deciding to eat near the station) — such consequential thoughts are symbolized by kha. Travelling elsewhere you might reflect on a collapsing brassware industry and whether it could be revived, though you are 'not personally affected' and 'not a direct player in your own thoughts' — such impersonal thoughts are also kha. Kha MEANS 'sky' but is NOT the acoustic root of the sky (that is ha); kha also means 'heaven', but only its CRUDE aspects — the sphere of heaven that transcends the crude is kṣa. Ka = Kārya Brahma is the first consonant; and since ka + ha = kha, kha immediately follows ka in the Indo-Aryan alphabet.
rows.attested_vs_authored_verbatim: ATTESTED: kha = cintā vṛtti; the personal (train) vs impersonal (industry) modes; kha ≠ the sky's root (ha is), kha = crude heaven vs kṣa = transcendent heaven; ka + ha = kha. AUTHORED: labelling anxious/gripping rumination as binding and composed impersonal openness as liberating applies the framework's fixation-vs-detachment principle (consistent with the source lexicon); the passage describes both modes as cintā without itself labelling them binding/liberating.

rows.binding_gloss: restless striving that cannot stop — effort compulsively driven on, unable to cease (and, clung to mundane ends, ceaseless outward striving)
rows.liberating_gloss: will-force applied to arouse one's dormant higher potential — purposeful effort that exerts and then rests into poised, alert repose without inertia; the effort behind spiritual elevation
rows.classical_or_philosophical_association_v: ceṣṭā = the effort to arouse dormant potentiality (latent genius -> applied will-force -> expression; else unexpressed). Described as the MAIN CAUSE of BOTH mundane development AND spiritual elevation, operating across the physical, psychic and spiritual spheres. (Scope/significance of the vṛtti — NOT a separate cosmological association.)
rows.primary_text_citation: Sarkar: Every entity has the potentiality of expression; an animate entity can arouse that dormant potentiality through both internal and external means. If poetic genius lies dormant in someone and he arouses it by applying his will-force, he becomes a renowned poet; if lethargy prevents it, the genius stays unexpressed. The effort made to arouse one's dormant potentiality is called ceṣṭā. Ceṣṭā is one of the psychic vṛttis and is the MAIN CAUSE of mundane development AND spiritual elevation — its value in the mundane and supramundane spheres is immense. Ga, the acoustic root of ceṣṭā, plays an important role in the physical, psychic and spiritual spheres.
rows.attested_vs_authored_verbatim: ATTESTED: ga = ceṣṭā vṛtti (effort to arouse dormant potential); its immense value in BOTH the mundane and supramundane spheres. AUTHORED: the binding/liberating split (restless-can't-stop striving vs poised effort-that-rests / spiritually-elevating will-force) applies the framework's restlessness-vs-poise principle (consistent with the source lexicon); the passage frames ceṣṭā as valuable in both spheres and does not itself label a binding pole.

rows.binding_gloss: mamatā bounded by the relative factors (time, space, individuality) — partial, possessive 'mine-ness' that clings to its own (own child, own country, own moment) while excluding or even harming what lies outside it
rows.liberating_gloss: mamatā made to TRANSCEND time, space and individuality — love expanded past its relative boundaries into universal affection that holds the loved on an open hand (achievable only by human beings, through persistent, intense effort)
rows.classical_or_philosophical_association_v: mamatā is related to time, space and individuality; its bounded form shows as place-attachment (praising one's own poor goods over better foreign ones — a 'psychic disease'), individuality (the mother who cherishes her child yet slices kai fish unmoved), and time (the cow that licks its calf today, kicks it away grown tomorrow). (Illustrations/scope of the vṛtti — not a separate cosmological association.)
rows.primary_text_citation: Sarkar: Mamatā, the vṛtti of love and attachment, is related to time, space and individuality. People praise even the poorest goods made in their own country and criticize the best goods made elsewhere — irrational attachment for a place, a psychic disease (SPACE). A mother who sacrifices everything for her child mercilessly slices living kai fish without feeling, deaf to their agony (INDIVIDUALITY). The mother cow who lovingly licks her calf today kicks it away when it grows tomorrow (TIME). Thus mamatā is limited by the relative factors. Only human beings can make mamatā TRANSCEND the boundaries of time, space and individuality, after persistent and intense effort — impossible for other beings. Gha is the acoustic root of mamatā vṛtti.
rows.attested_vs_authored_verbatim: ATTESTED — and unusually so: gha = mamatā vṛtti (love/attachment); its limitation by time/space/individuality; and that only humans can make it TRANSCEND those boundaries through effort. The binding (bounded attachment) vs liberating (boundary-transcending universal love) split is directly SUPPORTED by the passage's own bounded-vs-transcendent contrast — lighter authored component than most entries.

rows.binding_gloss: dambha as vanity — the self displayed and performed for others' eyes; conduct staged to be seen and admired
rows.liberating_gloss: conduct that stands without outward performance — action done for its own sake, needing no audience or applause
rows.classical_or_philosophical_association_v: Phonetic-historical (NOT poles): per the legend, una was learned by Vashiṣṭha in China and introduced to India, and is used across the Indo-Chinese languages (Tibetan/Ladakhi/Sherpa/Manpa). Its transmission is tied to the Tárā cult — but the Tárā deities have their OWN acoustic roots (aeṃ for Vajra/Nīla Tárā; krīṃ = ka[Kārya Brahma] + ra[luminous factor] for Bhrāmarī Tárā / Kālī), NOT una. Record as history/association; do not fold aeṃ/krīṃ/Tárā into nga's poles.
rows.primary_text_citation: Sarkar: Uṋa (ṅa) is the acoustic root of dambha vṛtti (vanity). The popular story: the sage Vashiṣṭha travelled to China to learn the Chinese school of Tantra, learned the use of una in Tantric mantras, and introduced it in India; una is used extensively across the Indo-Chinese languages (Tibetan, Ladakhi, Sherpa, Manpa). Its transmission is linked to the Tárā cult, trifurcated as Ugra/Vajra Tárā (India), Nīla Tárā / Nīla Sarasvatī (Tibet), and Bhrāmarī / Kṛṣṇa Tárā (China). The acoustic root of Vajra Tárā and Nīla Tárā is aeṃ; that of the black Bhrāmarī Tárā (= Kālī in Varṇāśrama Dharma) is krīṃ (ka = Kārya Brahma + ra = the luminous factor).
rows.attested_vs_authored_verbatim: ATTESTED: nga (uṋa/ṅa) = dambha vṛtti (vanity); the phonetic history (Chinese-origin legend, Indo-Chinese usage) and the Tárā-cult context with the deities' SEPARATE roots aeṃ/krīṃ. AUTHORED: the binding/liberating split (displayed-for-others vs conduct-without-performance) applies the framework's display-vs-unselfconscious principle (consistent with the source lexicon); the passage states the vṛtti but does not itself split it into poles.

rows.primary_text_citation: Sarkar: Ṭa is the acoustic root of vitarka vṛtti (overstating one's case). Vitarka is not merely debating; it means overstating one's case to the point of garrulousness — a combination of bad temper and garrulousness. It is NOT synonymous with kaśāya vṛtti (speaking harshly to hurt others). Example (Howrah station): asked whether the Uluberia local has left, one gentleman snaps abusively ('Am I a railway timetable?... People like you make life hell...') — uncontrolled vitarka; a second replies helpfully with just the relevant facts (platform eleven, five minutes) — pramita vāk (balanced statement, only relevant words).
